Patient Vignette: "Mark"

Mark is a 56-year-old married man, a former combat pilot who now flies commercial airliners. He presents as a tall, solidly built man with a still-military bearing, though his posture seems to collapse slightly when he sits down in the therapy office. He has been referred by his airline’s medical board following a mandatory evaluation after a near-fatal midair collision with a drone that occurred fourteen months ago.

The accident happened on a clear Tuesday afternoon. Mark was piloting a fully loaded passenger jet on a standard approach into a major hub. He remembers the sudden, violent crack as the drone punched through the cockpit windscreen. The decompression was immediate, a deafening roar of wind. Shards of Plexiglass sliced through his flight suit and into his left arm and cheek. The aircraft lurched, the controls going heavy and unresponsive as the autopilot disengaged. For what he estimates was twelve seconds, he genuinely believed he was going to die. He fought the yoke, blood streaming into his eye, shouting for his co-pilot to declare an emergency. He got the plane down, the landing gear groaning, the tires smoking. The cabin crew later told him the passengers had been screaming. He remembers none of that. He remembers only the silence that followed, the strange quiet of the engines winding down, and the trembling in his hands that wouldn’t stop.

In the months since, Mark’s life has become a series of careful, exhausting avoidances. He no longer watches the news, especially if there is any mention of aviation. He has stopped reading the airline’s safety bulletins, something he used to do religiously. He cannot stand the sound of a loud crack—a door slamming, a book dropping, a child hitting a baseball with a wooden bat. When he hears it, his body reacts before his mind can catch up: his heart slams into his ribs, his palms go slick with sweat, and he finds himself scanning the ceiling for falling debris. He has learned to sit with his back to the wall in restaurants, always near an exit.

The nightmares began almost immediately. They are not replays of the accident itself. They are worse. In the dreams, he is still in the cockpit, but the controls are made of rubber. His hands push the yoke, but it bends like a toy. The ground rushes up, and he cannot stop it. He wakes gasping, his sheets soaked, convinced for a terrifying moment that he is still falling. His wife, Sarah, has learned not to touch him when he wakes. He once threw her arm off him, hard, before he realized where he was.

At work, Mark has become a ghost. He flies the same routes, but the sky no longer feels like his home. It feels like a trap. He is hypervigilant on every approach, his eyes fixed on the horizon, scanning for the impossible shape of a drone. He has developed a ritual: before every landing, he mutters a silent count of the seconds until touchdown, a private mantra to prove to himself that time is still passing. His co-pilots have noticed he is quieter, more brittle. He snaps at them for small talk. He has stopped going to the crew lounge after flights, preferring to sit alone in the locked cockpit, staring at the instruments, waiting for his heart rate to slow.

He tells me he feels like a fraud. He has flown for thirty years, survived combat missions over hostile terrain, and yet he cannot get through a single approach without his hands shaking on the controls. He is terrified that one day, the shaking will be too much. He is terrified that his body will betray him at the worst possible moment. He is terrified that the sky is no longer his friend.

He has not told his union representative about the flashbacks. He has not told the airline’s medical officer about the intrusive image that comes to him at night: the shattered windscreen, the wind, the smell of hydraulic fluid and blood. He tells me these things instead, his voice flat, his eyes fixed on the floor. He is a man who has always been in control, and now he is losing it, second by second, in the very air he used to love.
